concept.name: Wide-Column Databases

relationships.description: Connects Wide-Column Databases to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Wide-column databases (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable) partition data by a row/partition key and sort rows inside each partition by clustering columns on an LSM-tree storage engine, trading ad-hoc joins for linear horizontal write scale.
spark.keyTakeaway: Design your table schema around exact read queries using bounded partition keys (<100 MB) and clustering keys—never model wide-column tables like normalized SQL tables.

concept.whyItMatters: When write throughput hits hundreds of thousands of events per second across multiple regions (IoT telemetry, messaging inboxes, time-series logs), single-leader B-tree databases hit lock contention and random disk I/O bottlenecks. Wide-column stores convert writes into sequential appends and scale linearly by adding nodes.
whenToUse: Write-heavy workloads (100K–1M+ writes/sec) such as time-series telemetry, activity feeds, or immutable event logs.
Predictable key-based lookups and range scans (e.g., 'last 50 messages for channel_id X sorted by timestamp DESC').
Multi-region active-active availability where tunable consistency (LOCAL_QUORUM) must survive rack or region failures.
whenNotToUse: Ad-hoc analytical queries, arbitrary `WHERE` filters across unindexed columns, or multi-table `JOIN`s.
Workloads requiring multi-row ACID transactions with serializable isolation across arbitrary keys.
High-churn update/delete-heavy queues where frequent deletes generate millions of tombstones that cripple read latency.
keyPoints: The primary key splits into `(partition_key, clustering_keys)`: the partition key hashes (e.g., Murmur3) to a replica set via consistent hashing, while clustering keys sort rows physically on disk within that partition.
Writes append sequentially to an on-disk CommitLog (WAL) and an in-memory Memtable, later flushing to immutable SSTables—making writes O(1) without random disk seeks.
Reads merge data across the Memtable and multiple SSTables using Bloom filters (typically ~1% false positive rate) and partition indexes, which background compaction periodically merges.
Tunable consistency uses `R + W > RF` (e.g., `RF=3` with `LOCAL_QUORUM=2` reads and writes) for strong consistency per partition, or `LOCAL_ONE` for maximum availability.
Deletes do not erase data immediately; they write **tombstone** markers that must be scanned during reads until `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) and compaction purge them.

examples.title: IoT Fleet Telemetry Ingestion (ScyllaDB + TWCS)
examples.scenario: A connected-vehicle platform ingests 500,000 GPS/sensor pings per second and queries the latest 24 hours per vehicle.
examples.outcome: Modeling `PRIMARY KEY ((vehicle_id, bucket_date), ts)` with `CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC)` and Time-Window Compaction (TWCS) keeps partitions under 8 MB and sustains 1.8ms p99 writes at `LOCAL_QUORUM`.

examples.title: Chat Message History (Cassandra Composite Partitioning)
examples.scenario: A messaging app originally keyed messages by `channel_id` alone; active channels grew past 200M rows (1.5 GB partitions), causing JVM GC pauses and read timeouts.
examples.outcome: Bucketing the partition key to `((channel_id, month_bucket), message_id DESC)` capped partition sizes below 25 MB and eliminated compaction OOMs.

tradeOffs.pro: Duplicating data into one table per query pattern guarantees single-partition O(1) + range-scan reads with zero joins.
tradeOffs.con: Writes must update multiple tables (logged batches or async CDC), increasing storage footprint and risking partial-update drift if not idempotent.

tradeOffs.pro: STCS minimizes write amplification for write-heavy workloads.
tradeOffs.con: STCS requires up to 50% free disk headroom for large merges and suffers higher read amplification than LCS (which needs ~10% headroom but 10–30x higher write I/O).

tradeOffs.pro: LOCAL_QUORUM (2 of 3 replicas) guarantees linearizable-per-partition reads of the latest acknowledged write within a datacenter.
tradeOffs.con: Doubles cross-AZ network traffic and fails writes if 2 of 3 replicas in that rack/AZ set are unreachable.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Partition Growth (Hot Partition)
failureModes.description: Keying a table by `tenant_id` or `sensor_id` without a time/shard bucket lets a single partition exceed 100 MB–1 GB, skewing disk/CPU onto 3 nodes and triggering OOMs during compaction.
failureModes.mitigation: Add a time or hash bucket to the partition key (`((entity_id, yyyymm), ts)`) to cap every partition under 10–50 MB.

failureModes.name: Tombstone Accumulation & Read Failure
failureModes.description: Using a wide-column table as a FIFO queue or writing `NULL` values creates millions of tombstones; reads hit `tombstone_failure_threshold` (100,000) and abort.
failureModes.mitigation: Avoid inserting `NULL`s (omit unset columns), use TTLs with TWCS for time-series expiration, and never model mutable job queues in Cassandra.

failureModes.name: Skipped Anti-Entropy Repair (Zombie Data)
failureModes.description: If a node is down longer than `hinted_handoff_window` (3h) and `nodetool repair` does not run within `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days), tombstones expire and deleted rows resurrect.
failureModes.mitigation: Automate incremental/subrange Merkle-tree repairs on a 3–7 day schedule, well inside `gc_grace_seconds`.

failureModes.name: Cross-Partition `IN` / `ALLOW FILTERING` Scans
failureModes.description: Issuing `WHERE partition_key IN (...)` with 100 keys or `ALLOW FILTERING` forces a coordinator node to scatter-gather across the entire cluster, spiking p99 latency.
failureModes.mitigation: Ban `ALLOW FILTERING` in production and issue parallel async single-partition queries from a token-aware driver.

commonMistakes: Designing tables around entities first and adding secondary indexes (`CREATE INDEX`) later—global/local secondary indexes in Cassandra scatter-gather across nodes and collapse at scale.
Inserting explicit `NULL` values for optional fields in prepared statements, silently generating a tombstone on every write.
Using `LOGGED BATCH` across different partition keys for bulk loading, turning a single coordinator into a bottleneck.
Running Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) past 60% disk utilization, leaving insufficient space for the largest SSTable merge.
Using `ALL` consistency in production, sacrificing availability whenever a single node restarts.

sections.content:
## The idea

Wide-column databases organize data as a distributed, sorted sparse map: `PartitionKey -> ClusteringKey -> ColumnName -> (Value, Timestamp)`. Consistent hashing (e.g., `Murmur3Partitioner`) maps the **partition key** to a token ring owned by `RF` replicas (typically `RF=3`), while **clustering columns** keep all rows of a partition physically sorted on disk.

Under the hood, each node uses an **LSM-tree** (Log-Structured Merge-tree): writes hit an append-only CommitLog and an in-memory Memtable, flushing sequentially to immutable **SSTables**. That design eliminates random B-tree page writes and scales write throughput linearly with node count.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `LOCAL_QUORUM` write and read on a 6-node Cassandra/ScyllaDB cluster (`RF=3`) for `PRIMARY KEY ((device_id, day), ts) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC)`:

1. **Token-Aware Routing**: The client driver hashes `(device_id, day)` via Murmur3 and sends the write directly to one of the 3 owning replicas as coordinator.
2. **Local Append & Replication**: The coordinator appends the mutation to its CommitLog + Memtable and forwards it in parallel to the other 2 replicas.
3. **Quorum Ack**: Once 2 of 3 replicas (`floor(3/2) + 1 = 2`) acknowledge, the coordinator returns `200 OK` to the client in ~1.5–3ms.
4. **Flush & Compaction**: When the Memtable fills, it flushes sequentially to an immutable SSTable with a Bloom filter (10 bits/key, ~1% FP) and partition summary.
5. **Range Read**: Reading the latest 50 events seeks directly to `(device_id, day)` in the Memtable + non-eliminated SSTables (via Bloom filters) and streams the top 50 sorted rows without scanning old days.

edges.title: Zero-hop token routing
edges.description: Driver hashes partition key locally to hit an owning replica directly.

edges.label: Replicate RF=3
edges.title: Parallel replica dispatch
edges.description: Sends mutation to all 3 replicas; waits for 2 ACKs for LOCAL_QUORUM.

edges.label: WAL + Memtable flush
edges.title: Sequential LSM persistence
edges.description: Appends to CommitLog and sorted Memtable, flushing immutable SSTables.

edges.label: Merge SSTables + purge
edges.title: Background compaction
edges.description: Merges overlapping SSTables, drops expired TTLs/tombstones, rebuilds Bloom filters.

edges.label: Merkle tree anti-entropy
edges.title: Scheduled replica repair
edges.description: Reconciles missed writes before gc_grace_seconds expires to prevent zombie data.

data.caption: Sequential CommitLog appends keep writes fast, while compaction and Merkle repairs keep reads bounded and replicas consistent.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Partition sizing and tunable consistency math
sections.content:
## Partition sizing and tunable consistency math

Two invariants govern wide-column stability:

1. **Quorum Overlap ($R + W > N$)**: With Replication Factor $N = 3$ per datacenter, `LOCAL_QUORUM` sets $W = 2$ and $R = 2$ ($2 + 2 = 4 > 3$). At least one replica in every read quorum holds the latest acknowledged write, guaranteeing last-write-wins (by microsecond client/coordinator timestamp) without cross-region latency.
2. **Partition Ceiling**: Keep partitions under **100 MB** (ideally **1–10 MB** and **<100,000 cells**). If a device emits 1 KB/sec, a single day is $86,400 \times 1\text{ KB} \approx 86.4\text{ MB}$—already near the danger zone, so bucket by 4-hour or 1-hour windows instead.

## Compaction strategies compared

| Strategy | Write Amplification | Read Amplification | Free Disk Headroom | Tombstone Reclamation | Best Workload |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Size-Tiered (STCS)** | Low (1x–4x) | High (many SSTables overlap) | **50% required** | Slow (waits for largest tier) | Heavy append/update with infrequent reads |
| **Leveled (LCS)** | High (10x–30x) | **Low** (90% reads hit 1 SSTable) | **10% required** | Fast (small fixed-size L1+ files) | Read-heavy lookups and frequent updates |
| **Time-Window (TWCS)** | **Lowest** | Low (for recent time ranges) | **10–20% required** | **Instant** (drops whole expired files) | Append-only time-series with fixed TTLs |

## Failure modes

- **Clock Skew Breaking Last-Write-Wins (LWW)**: Wide-column stores resolve concurrent cell updates using the highest write timestamp; NTP drift between app servers can silently cause older writes to overwrite newer ones.
- **Read Repair & Hinted Handoff Storms**: When an overloaded node flaps, coordinators accumulate gigabytes of hints; replaying hints on recovery can push the recovering node back into overload.
- **Tombstone Read Amplification**: Scanning a partition with 50,000 tombstones and 10 live rows still reads and discards all 50,000 markers in memory, spiking p99 read latency.

## Query-first data modeling

Follow a strict three-step modeling workflow:

1. **List Exact Queries First**: Enumerate every `SELECT` pattern (including sort order and pagination) before defining a single table.
2. **Pick Bounded Partition Keys**: Ensure every query specifies the full partition key (`=`) and optionally a range (`>=`, `<`) on clustering columns.
3. **Denormalize Deliberately**: If you need to look up users by `email` and by `user_id`, maintain two tables (`users_by_id`, `users_by_email`) rather than adding a secondary index.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Bound every partition key with a time or shard bucket so max partition size stays <50 MB.
- [ ] Use `LOCAL_QUORUM` for both reads and writes with `RF=3` per datacenter.
- [ ] Select TWCS for TTL-based time-series and LCS for read-heavy mutable datasets.
- [ ] Omit unset columns in `INSERT` statements instead of binding `NULL` to avoid tombstone generation.
- [ ] Schedule automated `nodetool repair` every 3–7 days (strictly < `gc_grace_seconds` = 10 days) and sync NTP/chrony.

interviewProblems.title: Wide-Column Databases
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Wide-Column Databases. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Wide-column databases (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable) partition data by a row/partition key and sort rows inside each partition by clustering columns on an LSM-tree storage engine, trading ad-hoc joins for linear horizontal write scale.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replica LSM Engine applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Compaction & Repair.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Compaction & Repair experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Add a time or hash bucket to the partition key (`((entity_id, yyyymm), ts)`) to cap every partition under 10–50 MB.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Design your table schema around exact read queries using bounded partition keys (<100 MB) and clustering keys—never model wide-column tables like normalized SQL tables.
Avoid trap: Designing tables around entities first and adding secondary indexes (`CREATE INDEX`) later—global/local secondary indexes in Cassandra scatter-gather across nodes and collapse at scale.
Avoid trap: Inserting explicit `NULL` values for optional fields in prepared statements, silently generating a tombstone on every write.
When to reach for it: Write-heavy workloads (100K–1M+ writes/sec) such as time-series telemetry, activity feeds, or immutable event logs.
When to reach for it: Predictable key-based lookups and range scans (e.g., 'last 50 messages for channel_id X sorted by timestamp DESC').

putItTogether.title: Putting Wide Column Databases Together
putItTogether.summary: Design your table schema around exact read queries using bounded partition keys (<100 MB) and clustering keys—never model wide-column tables like normalized SQL tables.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Wide Column Databases before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Modeling `PRIMARY KEY ((vehicle_id, bucket_date), ts)` with `CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC)` and Time-Window Compaction (TWCS) keeps partitions under 8 MB and sustains 1.8ms p99 writes at `LOCAL_QUORUM`.
